WHO Western Pacific Region

Traditional, complementary and integrative medicine in the Western Pacific Region

How national health systems across the Region recognise and support TCIM.

About this dashboard

TCIM is used widely across the Western Pacific Region. It spans Indigenous healing traditions and other knowledge passed on over generations, as well as complementary therapies and integrative services offered within health systems. For many communities it is part of how health and well-being are understood and cared for, often alongside conventional care.

This dashboard brings together what each country's profile shows about TCIM in its national health system, so that progress can be seen country by country and across the Region as a whole. Each profile looks at national policies, laws, plans and other public sources, and rates them against the 14 action areas of the latest WHO Regional Framework for Harnessing Traditional and Complementary Medicine for Achieving Health and Well-being in the Western Pacific (2022). The profiles cover national policy, the regulation of products and practitioners, how services are delivered, the reporting of harmful effects, and research.

Start with the for what the profiles show across the Region, or go to for a summary of each country. The dashboard is produced by the Division of Health Systems and Services at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific. It is intended for WHO staff, Member States and partners planning work on TCIM.

What it is for

  • Seeing how TCIM is recognised and supported in each country's health system
  • Seeing where TCIM connects with primary health care, and where links could be strengthened
  • Learning from what other countries have done
  • Following change over time against the 2022 Regional Framework
  • Showing where information is still missing

Where the information comes from

Country profiles drawn from national documents and other publicly available information, read alongside the Global Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034. Community practice and work not yet published may not be reflected.

How the bands are calculated

Each of the 14 Regional Framework action areas counts 1 when established, 0.5 when partly in place and 0 when not found, giving a total out of 14. Totals of 0–4.5 are shown as limited or not found, 5–9 as partially established and 9.5–14 as established. The bands summarise what is documented at national level; they are not a WHO indicator, a measure of health outcomes or a ranking of countries. Each rating can be checked in the action areas table further down this page and in each country profile.

How the overall profile is calculated

Each action-area rating is assigned a value: established = 1, partially established = 0.5, and limited or not found = 0. The 14 values are added to give a total out of 14. Totals from 0 to 4.5 are shown as limited or not found, 5 to 9 as partially established, and 9.5 to 14 as established. Each action area counts equally, so strategic actions with 4 action areas carry slightly more weight than those with 3. A rating of limited or not found reflects the evidence found in the profile search, not proof that no activity exists.

TCIM in the places people turn to for care

TCIM is woven into many people’s everyday care across the Western Pacific Region: a remedy made at home, advice from an elder or healer, a product from the pharmacy, a visit to a clinic. Having a service nearby does not always make it accessible: many things shape whether people can use it, from whether the care they want is offered at all to whether it feels right for them. The map shows the places people may turn to, in a rural area and in a town or city. Many people use more than one, such as a home remedy alongside a visit to the health centre. Each place has examples from the country profiles. Care can also cross borders, so some examples come from people living abroad and are marked as such.

On this page

About the data and methods

  1. SourcesNational policies, laws, plans and budgets, WHO global surveys and reports, research and news
  2. Country profileA desk review, with a source for each statement. It builds on the country's earlier reviews and covers changes in between. Some sources not in English were read with machine translation (Google Translate)
  3. RatingEach of the 14 Regional Framework action areas
  4. Total scoreOut of 14, with each action area counting equally
  5. DashboardThe regional overview and country profiles. Figures shown for every country aim to be recent and national, for TCIM as a whole; where none was found, the profile says so

Reading the ratings

A rating describes what national documents and public sources record, not what people experience. A service being in place does not mean that people can reach and afford it, or that they find it culturally safe. Some people travel further to a practitioner they trust. Rules alone cannot make a service culturally safe: who runs it, and how it is offered, matter as much.

The Global Strategy’s guiding principles call for ‘aligning health needs and the preferences, lifestyles and cultural beliefs of diverse populations’. In New Zealand, for example, a 2021 review of publicly funded rongoā services emphasised the right of the rongoā sector to determine how rongoā is offered, including where and with whom.

Data sources

  • National documentsHealth and other sector policies, strategies and plans, laws and regulations, budgets and official statements
  • WHO sourcesCountry responses to WHO's global surveys on traditional medicine, WHO global reports and regional publications
  • ResearchPeer-reviewed studies and other published research on TCIM use, safety and practice in each country
  • Other public informationNews and official media, and information from professional bodies, universities and non-government organisations
  • International data and agreementsUN population estimates for 2026, and the official lists of countries that have joined international agreements, such as the Nagoya Protocol

Glossary

Action area
One of the 14 more specific areas under the strategic actions, such as national policies or regulation of products. Each is rated in every profile.
Benefit sharing
Sharing fairly with communities and knowledge holders the benefits that come from using their traditional knowledge, or their plants and other genetic resources, usually on terms agreed before use. Also called access and benefit sharing.
Complementary medicine
Health care practices that are not part of a country's mainstream medicine. Where evidence-based, they can support mainstream care. Definition from the Global Strategy.
Culturally safe care
Care that the people receiving it, not only those providing it, find respects their culture, identity and beliefs. It depends on who provides the care and how, not only on whether a service exists.
Essential medicines list
A country's list of the medicines its health system should always have available, often based on WHO's Model List of Essential Medicines.
Free, prior and informed consent
The right of Indigenous peoples and local communities to give or withhold their consent, freely and with full information, before their lands, resources or knowledge are used.
Global Strategy
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034, which the country profiles are read alongside.
Good manufacturing practice
Rules on how medicines, including herbal products, are made and checked, so that every batch meets set quality standards.
Integrative medicine
An evidence-based approach that brings biomedical knowledge and practice together with traditional or complementary medicine, drawing on more than one discipline. Definition from the Global Strategy.
Model of care
An agreed national way of providing TCIM within health services, setting out which services are offered, where and by whom.
Nagoya Protocol
An international agreement on fair sharing of the benefits from using plants and other genetic resources, and related traditional knowledge.
Not found
Nothing was found in public sources. It does not mean that nothing exists, only that it was not documented publicly.
Pharmacovigilance
Monitoring and reporting the harmful effects of medicines, including herbal and other TCIM products, for example through WHO's Programme for International Drug Monitoring.
Primary health care
A whole-of-society approach to health that meets people's needs as early as possible and as close as possible to where they live, from prevention to treatment and care. It includes the first level of formal care, such as health centres and clinics. Definition based on WHO and UNICEF, A vision for primary health care in the 21st century (2018).
Public and private services
Public services are run or paid for by government, such as public hospitals and clinics, national health insurance or other government schemes. Private services are paid for by people themselves or by private insurance. Care within families and communities sits outside both.
Rating levels
Each action area is rated established (counting 1), partially established (0.5) or limited or not found (0). The 14 ratings add up to the profile's total out of 14. Limited or not found means no national mechanism was found in the profile search; it does not mean no activity exists.
Referral pathway
The agreed route by which patients are passed between TCIM practitioners and conventional health services, in either direction.
Regional Framework
The WHO Regional Framework for Harnessing Traditional and Complementary Medicine for Achieving Health and Well-being in the Western Pacific (2022), which every country profile is rated against.
Review point
One of the times a country's TCIM has been reviewed, so far 2011, 2020 and 2026. Change is measured from the first.
Strategic action
One of the Regional Framework's 4 areas of work: policies; quality and safety; coverage and access; and documentation, research and innovation.
TCIM
Traditional, complementary and integrative medicine. The dashboard uses TCIM throughout; T&CM (traditional and complementary medicine) appears only in official titles, such as those of the Regional Framework's strategic actions.
Traditional knowledge
In health, the knowledge, skills and practices a community develops and passes on from generation to generation, often as part of its cultural identity. Based on the Global Strategy's definition of traditional medical knowledge.
Traditional medicine
Systems of health care and well-being, whether written down or passed on orally, that grew from different historical and cultural contexts before biomedicine and continue to evolve with science. Definition from the Global Strategy.
UHC Service Coverage Index
How well essential health services reach the whole population, scored 0 to 100. WHO and the World Bank track it for Sustainable Development Goal indicator 3.8.1, and each profile shows it under country context.
WHO collaborating centre
An institution designated by WHO to carry out work that supports WHO's programmes, such as research or training.
WHO drug monitoring
WHO's Programme for International Drug Monitoring. Member countries send reports of suspected harmful effects of medicines, including herbal products, to a shared global database.
WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine
A global meeting on traditional medicine convened by WHO. At the second, in December 2025, countries pledged national commitments on traditional medicine, the latest public statement of what each plans to do. Progress is to be reported at the next Summit, in November 2027.
